Experts say responsibility mostly lies with software providers and organizations that serve customers. But there are basic steps everyone should take to protect themselves. 
USE MULTI-FACTOR AUTHENTIFICATION
MFA, or multi-factor authentication, requires two forms of verification to access a protected site, such as a password plus a text-based code or security key. Emily Austin, principal security researcher at cybersecurity firm Censys, recommended unique passwords for individual websites, and for people to monitor any transactions.
“But realistically, for situations like the PHP vulnerabilities, there really isn’t much an end user can do beyond hope the services they rely on either don’t use PHP or have people actively working on patching,” Austin said.
The PHP flaws are the latest in a series of severe software bugs made worse by increasingly capable and accessible large language models. Long-hidden flaws in widely used software, once too obscure or complex for humans to exploit, are now much easier to surface and weaponize.
MAKE HARDWARE UPDATES AUTOMATIC
Dan Guido, CEO and co-founder of cybersecurity firm Trail of Bits, recommended people “turn on automatic updates for your phone, computer, and home router.” Companies typically issue security updates when patches are available for known vulnerabilities, so installing them promptly limits the window for bad actors. 
Even so, consumers remain at the mercy of the services they rely on, Guido said.
“Someone visiting a website can do everything right, like use two-factor authentication, and still have their information exposed,” Guido said. “You can't patch your hospital's website.” 
Most of the work falls on companies running services, Guido said. “They need to deploy fixes faster and limit the damage that compromised systems can cause.”
Runa Sandvik, the founder of Granitt and a digital security expert, said people need to update apps and services on their devices whenever they're available, and to not forget about internet-connected devices around the house.
"I can see a scenario in which some people have some sort of IoT device at home that maybe doesn't get frequent updates, maybe doesn't get any updates at all," Sandvik said. "It's worth double checking with the vendor to see if there is anything available."
PATCH, PATCH, PATCH
Dr. Daniel Gardham, a lecturer at the Surrey Centre for Cyber Security and the University of Surrey, said organizations must know what software they run, patch promptly and check whether they've already been compromised. In the AI age, attackers have the advantage, Gardham added.
“Finding vulnerabilities is becoming faster and easier, but fixing them across the range of systems that rely on this software is much harder,” Gardham said. “How well organizations manage that gap will determine whether AI makes the internet safer or more vulnerable.” 
BEWARE OF SCAMMERS
Any time a major cybersecurity threat makes the news, scammers and cybercriminals will try to take advantage, said Nic Adams, co-founder and CEO of 0rcus, a cyberkinetics company.
Be wary of unsolicited links. "When these headlines hit, check the affected company's instructions by opening its app or typing its website address yourself," Adams said. "An urgent message telling you to 'secure your account' deserves extra scrutiny." 
YOUR MONEY IS SAFE
Banks have been preparing for this moment since frontier models came out, and have "worked extremely hard to ensure there is no more low-hanging fruit for the bad guys to go after," said Paul Benda, executive vice president of risk, fraud and cybersecurity at the American Bankers Association. 
However, Benda added, "we are in a new normal" in terms of cyber threats, and consumers need to be aware, especially in the wake of the PHP vulnerabilities, when shopping with random retailers or websites "where their security is not going to be as good as your bank." 
Benda said consumers should not reuse passwords across shopping sites, and should consider using passkeys where possible, which are digital keys specific to certain websites, that avoid the need to enter a password into a website and a phishing resistant.

SEOUL, Oct 23 : South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix said on Friday that it had suspended its review of a US initial public offering for its Solidigm subsidiary, citing financial market volatility and share price trends.
South Korea's financial regulator said earlier this week that the listing could run afoul of the country's dual-listing restrictions, which were tightened in July to strengthen shareholder protection.
SK Hynix said in a statement it would continue to explore ways to fund Solidigm's expansion and enhance shareholder value, including reviewing the timing, scale and financing of future investments.
"This decision does not reflect any change in Solidigm's growth prospects or investment needs," the company said.

The move brings an end, at least for now, to a potential fundraising option that Reuters reported could raise as much as $15 billion, highlighting the challenge of balancing investment needs driven by booming AI-related memory demand with growing concerns in South Korea over the impact of subsidiary listings on existing shareholders.
Despite strong business performance at both SK Hynix and Solidigm, the company said increased market volatility and a broader correction in semiconductor stocks had prompted it to reconsider the listing.
Shares in SK Hynix have fallen more than 30 per cent since the potential Solidigm IPO was reported in late September, compared with a 20 per cent decline in South Korea's benchmark KOSPI index over the same period.
The announcement could, however, help improve investor sentiment towards semiconductor stocks, said Han Ji-young, an analyst at Kiwoom Securities. Concerns over Meta's creditworthiness, a selloff in US AI stocks and pressure from oil prices had repeatedly weighed on markets, eroding investor confidence, he added.
GROWING SCRUTINY OVER DUAL LISTINGS
The decision also follows heightened regulatory scrutiny of the proposed listing. Financial Supervisory Service Governor Lee Chan-jin told a parliamentary hearing earlier this week that regulators were examining whether Solidigm's potential US initial public offering would require a review under domestic rules.
Solidigm, based in Rancho Cordova, California, is SK Hynix's US subsidiary specialising in NAND flash memory and solid-state drives.
SK Hynix had considered an IPO as one of several ways to finance Solidigm's expansion amid growing demand for memory chips driven by artificial intelligence.
The company said raising external capital through a listing could have boosted its cash flow, helping fund new production facilities while supporting shareholder returns through dividends, share buybacks and share cancellations.
It added that an IPO could have helped investors better recognise Solidigm's growth potential, which it said was not fully reflected in the parent company's valuation.
Shares of SK Hynix were down 1.3 per cent in morning trade, compared with a 2.3 per cent decline in the benchmark KOSPI.

Source: Reuters

items.summary: Nepal has expressed sadness over the death of a Nepali citizen killed by debris from an intercepted drone near Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oil field. Two expatriates were killed, while Pakistani and Indian ...
items.body:
Nepal condemns attacks on civilians after citizen killed by drone debris at Saudi oil field Nepal has expressed sadness over the death of a Nepali citizen killed by debris from an intercepted drone near Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oil field. Two expatriates were killed, while Pakistani and Indian nationals were injured. Nepal condemned attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure.
ANI | Updated: 23-10-2026 10:13 IST | Created: 23-10-2026 10:13 IST

Representative Image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways
AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Nepal's Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed deep sadness over the death of a Nepali citizen in Saudi Arabia. According to the ministry, the person was killed by debris from a drone that Saudi air defence systems intercepted over Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oil field a day earlier. In a statement posted on X, the ministry offered condolences to the bereaved family and wished a speedy recovery to all those injured. It reiterated Nepal's "unequivocal condemnation" of attacks targeting civilians and critical infrastructure.
The ministry said Nepal continues to call for the peaceful resolution of disputes through dialogue, negotiation and diplomatic engagement, which it described as the country's principled position. The statement did not name the victim, give his hometown or say whether arrangements were under way to repatriate his body. Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Energy said air defence systems intercepted a drone attempting to target one of the oil field's processing facilities in the Eastern Province on Wednesday morning. The attempted attack caused a fire in a contractor's vehicle outside the facility's perimeter, without affecting operations. The ministry said two expatriates, one Nepali and one Filipino, were killed, while a Pakistani and an Indian national were injured.
Saudi Arabia is a major destination for Nepali migrant workers, thousands of whom are employed across the country. The Saudi ministry's statement did not identify who launched the drone. The incident came amid a series of drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia attributed to Yemen's Houthi rebels. The United States ordered non-emergency embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia on Wednesday.
Shaybah produces around one million barrels of crude oil a day and is located close to the border with the United Arab Emirates. The field was also targeted in March, when Saudi forces said they had shot down ten drones heading towards it. The foreign ministry did not say whether it had contacted the family or Saudi authorities, or what consular support it would provide. Nepal's embassy in Riyadh and the Department of Foreign Employment have not yet commented publicly. (ANI)

Key Takeaways
AI Summary

Hollywood actor Tom Cruise has been selected to be bestowed with the 52nd AFI Life Achievement Award, Variety reported. The award will be given by the American Film Institute at a gala tribute, in a ceremony set to be held at the Dolby Theatre in Hollywood on April 24, 2027.
Considered the highest honour for a career in film, the AFI Life Achievement Award is given to a single honouree every year, recognising talent that has furthered the cinematic arts, demonstrated longevity and been acknowledged by scholars, critics, peers, and audiences. Speaking on the same, Chair of the AFI Board of Trustees Kathleen Kennedy shared, “Tom Cruise is a global icon. As an actor and producer, he brings an extraordinary commitment to everything he does. What I especially admire is his deep belief in movies and their ability to bring people together.” Kennedy added, “That passion has made him an extraordinary ambassador for American film around the world. It is AFI’s honour to present him with the 52nd AFI Life Achievement Award,” as quoted by Variety.
In a career spanning over five decades, Tom Cruise – a renowned actor, producer, and philanthropist has several hit titles to his name, including ‘Top Gun’, ‘Risky Business’, ‘Minority Report’, ‘Interview with the Vampire’, ‘A Few Good Men’, and the popular ‘Mission: Impossible’ films. He will be seen next in the next chapter of ‘Days of Thunder’ alongside Anne Hathaway.
Cruise also received several accolades in his career, including Best Actor nods for his work on ‘Born on the Fourth of July’ and ‘Jerry Maguire’. He recently won a nomination as a producer of ‘Top Gun: Maverick’, which was also nominated for Best Picture. (ANI)

items.title: GM cancels deal with new US rare-earth magnet plant, documents say
items.author: Eric Onstad
items.creator: Eric Onstad
items.summary: General Motors , the biggest customer of a US factory making rare earth magnets for electric vehicles, cancelled its long-term supply deal with the manufacturer, and the two sides are in arbitration, according to regulatory documents and a person with knowledge of the situation.
items.body:
General Motors (GM.N) , the biggest customer of a US factory making rare earth magnets for electric vehicles, cancelled its long-term supply deal with the manufacturer, and the two sides are in arbitration, according to regulatory documents and a person with knowledge of the situation.
The move spotlights the challenges Western firms face in building domestic rare-earths output and cutting their reliance on China, which produces about 90% of global permanent magnets.
It also shows how the US auto industry's landscape has changed since Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025 and cut federal support for electric vehicles.
Germany's Vacuumschmelze, or VAC, signed a [USN:L8N34F3IX TEXT:"long-term deal"] in 2023 with GM to supply permanent magnets for its electric vehicles from a new plant in South Carolina.
Energy Fuels (UUUU.A) , which agreed in June to pay $1.9 billion to [USN:L4N42V0QM TEXT:"acquire VAC"], said in US Securities and Exchange Commission documents filed last week that a customer of the plant terminated its supply agreement on July 1, and VAC launched arbitration proceedings against that customer several days later.
It did not name the customer, but GM this week reported in an SEC filing that a supplier of a component for EV traction motors "initiated an arbitration against us seeking damages after we terminated a strategic sourcing agreement," without saying why it cancelled the deal.
The person familiar with the matter confirmed GM was the customer that cancelled the contract with VAC's US unit, e-VAC Magnetics.
GM and Energy Fuels declined to comment on the arbitration because it is confidential.
The dispute has not been previously reported and none of the companies involved have issued press releases about the issue.
VAC launched its $500-million US magnet plant late last year with a capacity of just under 2,000 metric tons a year, and 90% was set to be sold to GM, with the remainder supplying the US government, VAC CEO Erik Eschen [USN:L5N3UY0MF TEXT:"told Reuters"] in September last year.
VAC's US unit said it was seeking damages in arbitration due to wrongful termination.
"We have no concerns about VAC’s commercial success and its ability to produce rare earth permanent magnets to customer specifications," Energy Fuels said.
However, Energy Fuels told Reuters there may be "potential adjustments to our purchase price of VAC depending on the outcome of the arbitration."
GM ROLLS BACK EV SALES GM has been pulling back on sales of EVs, which historically have lost money, following the Trump administration’s withdrawal of incentives and tax breaks meant to benefit the industry.
In January, GM took a [USN:L6N3Y915L TEXT:"$6 billion charge"] to unwind some EV investments. When GM and VAC announced the supply deal three years ago, VAC said the plant would support GM for a minimum of 10 years and supply a wide range of models.
The dispute first arose in April 2026, according to the SEC documents. Energy Fuels said it was aware of the dispute when it was negotiating the VAC acquisition.
Energy Fuels, a producer of uranium for the nuclear power industry, said the takeover would allow it to become one of the world's largest non-Chinese producers of magnets used in the aerospace, defence and renewable energy sectors.
VAC supplies magnets to more than 1,000 customers, from facilities in Germany, Malaysia and other countries.

items.summary: US President Donald Trump launched a blistering attack against Tehran, accusing the Iranian leadership of manufacturing crises to artificially hike global crude oil prices ahead of the upcoming United ...
items.body:
"Iran doing everything to drive up oil prices ahead of midterms": Trump lashes out at Tehran regime US President Donald Trump launched a blistering attack against Tehran, accusing the Iranian leadership of manufacturing crises to artificially hike global crude oil prices ahead of the upcoming United States midterm elections and reaffirming that Iran must never be allowed to acquire nuclear capabilities.
ANI | Updated: 23-10-2026 10:11 IST | Created: 23-10-2026 10:11 IST

US President Donald Trump (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways
AI Summary

Analyzing article...

US President Donald Trump launched a blistering attack against Tehran, accusing the Iranian leadership of manufacturing crises to artificially hike global crude oil prices ahead of the upcoming United States midterm elections and reaffirming that Iran must never be allowed to acquire nuclear capabilities. In a sharply worded post shared across his social media channels, Trump dismissed allegations of major disruptions in the Persian Gulf, asserting that oil shipments through the critical maritime corridor remain elevated.
"Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the U.S. Midterm Election. They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict," Trump said. Labelling the dispensation in Tehran an "evil regime", Trump accused authorities of carrying out brutal, lethal crackdowns against civilian protesters on a mass scale.
"They continue to kill protestors, and anyone else that happens to be in their way. It is truly an Evil Regime, and I can only hope the American Public, and the World, understands how EVIL they are! 75,000 protestors lie dead in less than seven months," the US President claimed. Lashing out at domestic political opponents and the broader international community for what he termed an indifferent posture, Trump drew a firm red line regarding Tehran's atomic program.
"It is shocking how the World, and the Dumocrat Party, seem not to care. IRAN CAN NEVER HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON, AND THEY WILL NEVER A NUCLEAR WEAPON!" Trump wrote. Meanwhile, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy issued a warning to the United States over what it described as efforts to encourage vessels to pass through a mined maritime passage.
In a statement attributed to the IRGC Navy Command, the force accused Washington of encouraging ships to navigate the passage despite the presence of mines and warned that continued actions could widen the confrontation to US military bases in the region. "The arrogant US regime's insistence on inciting vessels to pass through the illegally mined passage has increased maritime accidents day by day, and the aggressive US military should know that if this trend continues, the scope of the confrontation will extend to the aggressive bases in the region. This is a serious warning," the IRGC Navy Command said.
The statement comes as Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy has claimed that it struck and set fire to four ships carrying oil cargoes in the northern Persian Gulf, while three other vessels collided with mines in the western Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian state media, Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB). In a statement issued on Thursday, the IRGC Navy said the four ships had previously crossed an "illegal route" despite warnings to the maritime companies operating them.
Earlier, US President Donald Trump on Wednesday (local time) said that the United States is not negotiating with Iran and "something" will happen "fairly soon." (ANI)

NEW YORK: US stocks tumbled on Thursday (Oct 22) and the Nasdaq posted its steepest daily drop since early June as a batch of high-profile earnings reports ignited fresh fears about the AI spending race.
The S&P 500 ended deep in negative territory. But the tech-laden Nasdaq , dragged down by microchips, suffered a steeper loss, falling 2.6 per cent in the wake of a spate of high-profile AI-related earnings results.
The blue-chip Dow eked out a nominal gain minutes before the closing bell.
Meta Platforms' results beat analyst expectations, but its stock slid 7.0 per cent as the Facebook parent posted its first cash outflow in more than a decade due to its AI-related expenditures and announced plans to issue non-voting shares in a two-for-one split to raise capital to spend on the nascent technology.

Tesla shares fell 3.1 per cent even though the electric car maker unexpectedly posted positive free cash flow in the quarter and cut its 2026 capital spending plans.
The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index .SOX , which has driven much of the current bull market's gains, plunged 6.7 per cent , its biggest daily percentage drop since June 23.
With Thursday's decline, the SOX is off more than 26 per cent from its record closing high reached on Jun 22, yet it remains up 51.5 per cent so far this year. The S&P 500 has risen 11.9 per cent over the same period.
"It's a wonderful day on Wall Street," said Paul Nolte, senior wealth adviser & market strategist at Murphy & Sylvest in Elmhurst, Illinois. "The only part of the market that is really suffering here is technology, which has been the golden child of the markets up until about June."
"Investors are starting to realize that there are some holes in the AI story," Nolte added. "And that's having an impact on the indices because they're so heavily weighted toward technology."
On the geopolitical stage, Iran-backed Houthis launched new strikes against Saudi targets, sending crude prices to a five-month high. Investors worried that ongoing Middle East strife could keep inflation hot and force the US Federal Reserve to keep raising interest rates.
Data from the Labour Department showed initial claims for unemployment benefits kept drifting along near multi-decade lows. Signs of labor market stability will allow the Fed to focus on fighting inflation. Financial markets are currently pricing in the probability that the central bank will raise its policy rate by another 25 basis points before year-end.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average .DJI rose 11.89 points, or 0.02 per cent, to 52,867.98, the S&P 500 .SPX lost 93.74 points, or 1.21 per cent, to 7,663.43 and the Nasdaq Composite .IXIC lost 694.00 points, or 2.60 per cent, to 26,008.86.

Related:

Commentary: Every investment portfolio looks like the same trade - AI

Third-quarter earnings season is well underway, with 111 of the companies in the S&P 500 having reported. Of those, 83 per cent have beaten analyst expectations, according to the most recent LSEG data.
Procter & Gamble warned that rising cost pressures would take an increasing bite out of profit, but beat analyst estimates, sending the stock 5.6 per cent higher and supporting consumer staples .SPLRCS .
Blackstone advanced 8.4 per cent , after the company said widening credit spreads on AI-related debt could present an opportunity to lock in higher returns.
Lockheed Martin climbed 7.0 per cent after the aerospace/defense firm raised its annual sales and profit forecast.
Spotify rose 11.1 per cent after the Swedish music streaming firm forecast fourth-quarter profit above Wall Street estimates, betting on its AI-powered features to drive user growth.
Union Pacific gained 3.6 per cent following the company's quarterly earnings beat, which was helped by core pricing gains, although the railroad flagged a hit from rising fuel prices.
Chipmakers Intel, AMD, Sandisk and Marvell all tumbled more than 8 per cent amid the broader semiconductor selloff.
Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.01-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 173 new highs and 366 new lows on the NYSE.
On the Nasdaq , 2,022 stocks rose and 2,766 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.37-to-1 ratio.
The S&P 500 posted 40 new 52-week highs and four new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 82 new highs and 342 new lows.
Volume on US exchanges was 18.79 billion shares, compared with the 17.19 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days.

WASHINGTON, Oct 22 : The Federal Communications Commission said on Thursday it has granted a waiver to Intel from its ban on some foreign-made advanced robotics.
The FCC said it would grant a one-year waiver of its rules in order to prevent "potential disruptions in the availability of domestic semiconductor manufacturing services for Intel’s customers."
Intel in a petition last week said the robotic devices are critical to its US semiconductor manufacturing. Without the waiver, Intel would not have been allowed to make software, firmware, and hardware changes for its "Automated Guided Vehicles" that it said could be classified by the agency as robots.
Intel told the FCC there is a lack of proven domestic alternatives that meet operational requirements and replacing the automated guided vehicles would take Intel years and could disrupt its manufacturing operations.

The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The vehicles are used to transport materials within Intel's semiconductor facilities and have been in operation for over two decades, the company said.
In July, the FCC barred imports of new Chinese robots and power inverters, seeking to protect the US AI buildout from national security threats and reshore key industries slated for explosive growth.
The FCC barred imports of new Chinese humanoid and quadruped robots, in addition to connected power inverters. The FCC has since granted some approvals to allow for continued specific robotic device imports.
Some analysts forecast broad adoption of humanoid robots, topped with AI-enabled "brains," in consumer and industrial arenas, while explosive data-center construction in the US will depend on reliable sources of inverters.

items.title: Sharp drops for AI stocks overwhelm markets worldwide as oil prices jump
items.author: The Associated Press
items.summary: Drops for stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are dragging down markets worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May because of worries about the war with Iran ...
items.body: NEW YORK — The latest shudder for stocks in the artificial intelligence industry pulled markets lower worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May on worries about the war with Iran. The S&P 500 fell 1.2 per cent for its worst day since July, while the Nasdaq composite tumbled 2.6 per cent. The weakness for tech stocks was so overwhelming that it masked strength for the rest of the U.S. market, where the majority of stocks actually rose. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 11 points, or less than 0.1 per cent. AI-related stocks have been swinging on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build data centers and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain that their prices shot too high following a yearslong frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth. Lam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock’s price, but Lam Research’s tumbled 11.8 per cent. It gave a range for its forecast for profit this quarter whose midpoint was slightly below analysts’ expectations. Its stock also came into the day with a 52.4 per cent surge for the year so far, nearly quadruple the gain for the overall S&P 500, leaving plenty of room for potential disappointment. Other big tech stocks likewise fell following quarterly reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets. Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7 per cent after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it’s creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses. Tesla fell 3.1 per cent after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast. The global tide against AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 4.4 per cent. Because the chip giant is the largest company on Wall Street by total value, movements for its stock carry more weight on the S&P 500 than any other, and it was the single strongest force pulling the index lower. CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 10.1 per cent. The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where indexes are full of players in the industry. South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.5 per cent, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 3 per cent and Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 2.7 per cent. Also weighing on global stock markets was a jump in oil prices. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil leaped 4 per cent to US$113.17 after touching its highest level in five months. It’s shot up from less than US$97 at the start of the month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal. In Europe, France’s CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent’s sharpest losses with a drop of 1.4 per cent. It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or U.S. indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds. Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government’s big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt. Worries about big government debt are weighing on almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong U.S. economy and other factors, have pushed yields in the U.S. bond market recently to their highest levels in decades. But U.S. yields nevertheless fell sharply Thursday in a signal that investors were buying U.S. government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled. The yield on the 10-year Treasury tumbled to 4.97 per cent from 5.13 per cent late Wednesday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier this month. That’s a major move for the bond market. Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the U.S. economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could signal that layoffs remain low across the country. That solid economy has helped U.S. companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the U.S. stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. Two out of every three stocks within the S&P 500 rose Thursday, only to get drowned out by the drops for more influential tech stocks. Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses Thursday. CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expects “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 5.6 per cent. All told, the S&P 500 fell 93.74 points to 7,663.43. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 11.89 to 52,867.98, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 694.00 to 26,008.86. ___ Stan Choe, The Associated Press AP Business Writer Elaine Kurtenbach contributed to this report.

items.title: Canada Post CEO touts ‘early signs’ of recovery even as financial woes persist
items.author: The Canadian Press
items.summary: The head of Canada Post says it is showing “early signs” of financial recovery despite falling revenue and bigger losses in the first half of the year.
items.body: Canada Post has begun to show “early signs” of financial recovery, its CEO says, as the beleaguered Crown corporation starts to step back from the fiscal cliff. At its annual public meeting, Doug Ettinger said Canada Post is winning back some of the parcel delivery market that has slipped away since 2019. To make those gains, the Crown corporation is giving shipping discounts to small businesses and pushing a new direct-to-consumer online marketplace. “I am extremely confident that the organization is not only trending in the right direction, it is poised to re-establish itself as a crucial infrastructure built to serve Canada,” Ettinger said, invoking national sovereignty to make the case for a healthy postal service. However, its network of post offices remains “overbuilt” in cities and must be scaled down, he said Thursday.  Ettinger qualified that Canada Post will continue to serve rural and remote communities. “We will not abandon the small communities that rely on us.” Switching the remaining four million addresses that still enjoy doorstep delivery to community mailboxes within about five years marks a key pillar of Canada Post’s plan to overhaul its business model in the face of declining letter mail and financial losses. The Crown corporation launched an online tool Thursday that lets customers with door-to-door delivery enter their postal code to see when their area is slated for conversion to a community mailbox. The first such switch in more than 10 years was completed a few days ago in Winnipeg and Sept-Îles, Que., executives said. By the end of 2027, about 700,000 more households from Halifax to Victoria will be collecting their mail from the compact aluminum boxes, according to Canada Post. In August, the organization reported losses of $277 million before taxes for the second quarter of the year, marking an improvement from $407 million pre-tax loss a year earlier. The three-month period revealed “signs of an early turning point,” said chief financial officer Rindala El-Hage, as revenue rose — from parcels in particular — and operating costs plummeted. “These results do not resolve our structural challenges, but they show that ... the trajectory can improve,” she said. Ettinger twice referred to the “fiscal cliff” the service still faces and pointed the finger at successive governments for a sluggish response. “This is not where any of us wanted to be,” said the chief executive. But Ettinger, who is slated to step down at the end of his second term in March, said the current government under Prime Minister Mark Carney has opened the door to overdue shifts, such as lifting the moratorium on new community mailboxes imposed by his predecessor in 2015. Other reforms include weekend parcel delivery — under a staggered rollout across the country that kicked off this month — and expected post office closures. To win over small businesses, they will continue to receive Canada Post’s biggest shipping discounts no matter how small the volume through the end of the year. A 15 per cent discount on fuel surcharges for domestic parcels eases the pain of price hikes tied to the soaring price of gas and diesel. A new online marketplace dubbed Canada Shops is also in the testing phase. Launched over the summer, it aims to connect Canadian retailers with domestic shoppers. Between 2019 and 2023, the postal service’s share of the parcel market plummeted to 29 per cent from 62 per cent, as Amazon and other competitors seized on skyrocketing demand for next-day deliveries. “This isn’t about competing with other marketplace giants,” said chief marketing officer Rod Hart of the direct-to-consumer platform. The update from Canada Post comes less than five months after postal workers approved a tentative agreement that will boost their wages nearly 10 per cent in the first 24 months of the five-year deal. The green light given by most of the union’s 55,000 employees followed more than two years of labour strife. Greater use of community mailboxes, which reduce the need for letter carriers, was among the sticking points. In December 2024, the federal government asked the Canada Industrial Relations Board to step in to quash a month-long strike, and struck an Industrial Inquiry Commission to find a path forward. That probe, led by William Kaplan, made a series of recommendations that were later adopted and rolled out in a suite of sweeping changes to Canada Post’s mandate. Announced in September 2025, the overhaul lifted the community mailbox moratorium and ended the freeze on rural post office closures — some locations are now surrounded by suburban subdivisions — that had been in place since 1994, covering close to 4,000 outlets. --- Christopher Reynolds, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

items.title: Apple launches into foldable market as iPhone Duo sales begin
items.author: Aditya Soni
items.creator: Aditya Soni
items.summary: Sales of Apple's first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, began on Friday, with market watchers betting on whether the device can reinvent the small foldables market in the same way the iPhone did for smartphones.
items.body:
Sales of Apple's (AAPL.O) first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, began on Friday, with market watchers betting on whether the device can reinvent the small foldables market in the same way the iPhone did for smartphones.
The Duo's reception could prove an early test for new CEO John Ternus, the former hardware chief who unveiled the phone barely a week after taking charge in September.
It could also have large implications for a niche category in which rivals such as Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and Huawei Technologies have sold premium offerings for several years.
Within minutes of pre-orders opening last Friday, Apple's estimated delivery dates for the Duo had slipped to late January as demand outpaced supply. The US company called the response from customers "nothing short of extraordinary."
With the massive demand, Apple capped pre-orders at two handsets per customer and limited sales significantly for walk-in shoppers, resulting in muted crowds unlike the hype that typically accompanied new iPhone releases.
In China, France, Hong Kong, India and Japan, units would be available only for customers who had ordered online
In Sydney, the first Apple store to sell the phones on Friday, a queue of customers formed outside before opening at 8 a.m. local time (2100 GMT).
Simon Krishnan, a 48-year-old engineer, paid A$3,899 ($2,734) for a Duo with 512GB memory.
"This is a bit of a luxury item for me, because it's so expensive, but I just think, you know what? Life's too short," he said.
In China, a soft consumer market combined with memory costs pushing prices higher has led to [USN:P8N44H02N TEXT:"six straight quarters"] of declines in smartphone shipments. Apple's market share, however, has rebounded as some phone buyers trade up to premium devices while others seek value at the lower end of the market, putting pressure on mid-range brands.
Liu Wei, a 26-year-old healthcare professional, already has a foldable phone from Xiaomi (1810.HK) , but still queued outside a central Shanghai Apple store from 6 a.m. to get his hands on Apple's first foldable.
"I've used Apple products for many years and I have more trust (in the brand), so I bought one on launch day to try it out," he said.
In Hong Kong, May, 38, who declined to give his full name for privacy reasons, secured a 256GB iPhone Duo, which retails for HK$17,499 ($2,231.73), during an online pre‑sale and aimed to resell the handset for a profit of around HK$4,000: “A few meals' worth of money,” he joked.
MIXED REVIEWS Early reviews have praised the Duo's design as well as its sturdy and barely visible hinge, a major feat for phones whose prominent creased screen has long been a drawback and potential deterrent for buyers.
But reviewers have said camera compromises including the absence of a telephoto lens and third-party apps that still need to be reworked for the new display size could disappoint some buyers. They have also said the Duo in its smaller, folded state is less handy for the litany of quick tasks that most users carry out each day on standard iPhones, with several prominent reviewers recommending against the Duo for many Apple customers.
"It's been a lot of fun trying the Duo out for a week, but it feels like I've gotten to use an extraordinarily polished prototype — not a finished product that I'd want to buy and carry," longtime Apple commentator John Gruber, author of the blog Daring Fireball, wrote in a review.
Tech commentator Marques Brownlee, popularly known as MKBHD, said in a YouTube review that "if you're just a regular person who doesn't do much more than texting, social media and browsing here and there, then it is probably a no. But if the $2,000 doesn't mean much to you, and you like the idea, after the learning curve and getting used to not having facial identification, it is a really fun phone."
TOUGH TO FIND The limited supplies could disappoint Apple fans lining up in front of stores to buy the Duo. Apple told Reuters that walk-in availability would vary by country, with limited stocks in the US, Australia, Canada, Mexico and much of Britain and Europe.
"Foldables have been an established category for years, but adoption has remained relatively limited compared with conventional smartphones. Apple's entry could bring the format to a much broader audience," said Francisco Jeronimo, vice president at market researcher IDC.
IDC expects Apple will take 44% of the foldable value in 2026 on 31% of foldable units. By 2027, it will become the market leader in the category both in value and units shipped, IDC forecast.
"Apple has made a convincing case for this form factor," Jeronimo said after spending a week with the passport-shaped Duo.
"Now comes the next test: turning excitement into availability, adoption and a lasting new chapter for the smartphone market," Jeronimo said.
($1 = 1.4257 Australian dollars)
($1 = 7.8410 Hong Kong dollars)

Steep bill for AI buildout punishes Meta, other tech favorites

FAST

NEW YORK, Oct 22 : The tab for the next round of the AI buildout came due on Thursday.
Investors sold shares of Meta Platforms and a wealth of companies central to the AI trade, a day after Meta — one of the hyperscalers spending billions to build data centers and other infrastructure supporting the AI boom — said it would issue a new class of shares that will help it raise funds. 
Meta fell 7 per cent, its largest drop since July. SpaceX declined 9 per cent and semiconductor company Nvidia — a bellwether of the AI trade — dropped 4 per cent. The Nasdaq Composite lost 2.6 per cent, its largest decline since June 5. 
Sentiment was also hurt by a 12 per cent plunge in shares of semiconductor company Lam Research following its results. The Philadelphia Semiconductor index lost 6.7 per cent.

The pullback is the latest test for the AI trade as investors focus on the rising costs of long-term projects where the payoff remains uncertain.
Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending, but Wall Street now expects that the rise in borrowing costs will motivate tech companies like Meta to sell billions of dollars in stock to fund the next round of building.
That dilution could put pressure on share prices, and is a potentially unwelcome development when major US stock indexes remain near all-time highs despite a punishing month of volatile trading.
RETURN ON INVESTMENT CONCERNS
Selling started with "the big question about the (return on investment) on all the spending," said Matthew Maley, chief market strategist at Miller Tabak. "It's just becoming more and more evident to people that it's going to take a lot longer." 
Thomas Hayes, chairman at Great Hill Capital LLC in New York, agreed that ROI concerns are central while also citing remarks by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang about a financing bottleneck for smaller AI companies as contributing to the selling. 
Meta said on Wednesday it would use new Class C shares, which hold no voting power, to fund AI spending and other priorities. Meta also raised the low end of its annual spending forecast to $135 billion from $130 billion, with the high end unchanged at $145 billion.
That level of spending will require lots of investor participation in coming stock sales. Meta reported negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion in the third quarter, compared with positive free cash flow of $10.63 billion a year earlier. It was the first cash burn at Meta in more than a decade.
“More spending, negative free cash flow, not enough revenue being generated from the spend (is) concerning investors that this is just sort of a bit of a money pit,” said Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth in Fairfield, Connecticut.
The action highlights concern over how AI investment will be paid for. Credit default swaps, which track perceived default risk for the debt of the biggest AI players, have largely risen over the past year, with Meta’s hitting a record on Thursday.
INVESTOR ANXIETY SHOWS
Fresh signs of market anxiety over AI spending snowballed into a broad market selloff Thursday, with some saying an AI pullback could hit US growth. Investors sought the safety of Treasury bonds, sending those prices higher.
"This is your classic rotation day,” said Joe Saluzzi, partner, co-founder and co-head of equity trading at Themis Trading in Chatham, New Jersey. “You can see the money going into Treasuries, so it's a classic safety move ... They are rotating out of techs, out of the AIs, and into the more safety trades, whether it's bonds or some of those big Dow Jones stocks.”
Thursday’s selloff added to the pressure on the neocloud companies at the heart of the AI buildout, with Nebius off 7 per cent after announcing a new $3.5 billion credit line from Citigroup and CoreWeave, whose unsecured bond yields soared to 15 per cent in last week’s AI selloff, down 10 per cent.
Bank of America analyst Tal Liani said in a report on Thursday he is maintaining a buy rating and a price target of $140 on CoreWeave stock heading into next month’s earnings report, though he said he believes the firm will need to raise $20 billion to fund commitments to customers — the sort of prospect that is generating anxiety among tech investors. 
"Nobody is worried about Meta or Amazon or Google getting the financing they need," Maley said. "But if it gets prohibitive for smaller companies, then you don't have to have an implosion of things to make people nervous."

Source: Reuters

FAST

US President Donald Trump criticised NBA superstar LeBron James on Thursday (Oct 23) for what he called disrespectful behaviour during the singing of the national anthem at a recent NBA game.
"While listening to our National Anthem, LeBron James disrespects our Country," Trump said in a Truth Social post accompanied by a video showing James moving his body during the singing of the anthem. "LeBron James should apologise to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!"
The clip Trump shared showed James standing in line with the members of the Philadelphia 76ers, swinging his arms in a warmup-type stretch and performing basketball shooting movements.
A representative for the 76ers did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Trump has repeatedly criticised athletes for their behaviour during pre-game renditions of the US national anthem, notably beginning with NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick's kneeling protest in support of racial justice.
Trump cancelled a planned White House visit of the Super Bowl champions Philadelphia Eagles in 2018 after the team disagreed with his call for players to stand during the anthem.
James became a leading voice in the Black Lives Matter movement in 2020 and has frequently supported progressive issues as he ascended to the top of the NBA's all-time scoring list.

items.title: Kering-Le recul des ventes de Gucci au T3 pèse sur les espoirs de relance
items.author: Tassilo Hummel, Alessandro Parodi, Elena Smirnova
items.creator: Tassilo Hummel, Alessandro Parodi, Elena Smirnova
items.summary: Le groupe de luxe français Kering a annoncé jeudi une baisse des ventes de Gucci au troisième trimestre, la faiblesse persistante de la fréquentation de ses magasins compliquant les efforts de redressement engagés par son directeur général Luca de Meo.
items.body:
Le groupe de luxe français Kering (PRTP.PA) a annoncé jeudi une baisse des ventes de Gucci au troisième trimestre, la faiblesse persistante de la fréquentation de ses magasins compliquant les efforts de redressement engagés par son directeur général Luca de Meo.
[USN:L8N40Z0D8 TEXT:"Luca de Meo"], vétéran de l'industrie automobile qui a pris les rênes du groupe l'an dernier, tente de redresser Kering à travers un plan stratégique sur cinq ans visant à doubler sa marge opérationnelle. Mais les tensions au Moyen-Orient, la faiblesse de la demande en Chine et le ralentissement de la dynamique de consommation aux États-Unis compliquent la réalisation de cet objectif.
Les ventes trimestrielles inférieures aux attentes publiées récemment par [USN:L8N45Y1DP TEXT:"LVMH"] et [USN:L8N4680BW TEXT:"Hermès"], ainsi que les signes d'un ralentissement de la demande aux États-Unis, ont renforcé les inquiétudes des investisseurs quant au redressement de Kering.
Interrogée lors d'une conférence téléphonique sur la possibilité d'un retour à la croissance du groupe cette année, la directrice financière Armelle Poulou n'a pas souhaité commenter les perspectives, renvoyant à la publication des résultats annuels.
Les certificats américains de dépôt (ADR) de Kering ont chuté de 11% après la publication de l'activité trimestrielle du groupe.
Les ventes de Gucci, qui représentent environ la moitié du résultat opérationnel du groupe, se sont établies à 1,29 milliard d'euros au cours du trimestre. Sur l'ensemble du groupe, le chiffre d'affaires a reculé de 1% à données comparables.
Selon Kering, la principale difficulté de Gucci reste la baisse de la fréquentation des magasins, particulièrement en Chine. Les ventes de la marque ont également légèrement reculé en Amérique du Nord.
Pour attirer davantage de clients dans les magasins Gucci, Kering prévoit d'accroître ses investissements dans le marketing et l'expérience client, a déclaré Armelle Poulou.
"Nous poursuivons l'exécution de notre plan avec la plus grande discipline", a déclaré Armelle Poulou. Elle a ajouté que le groupe avait déjà réduit son réseau de distribution de 105 magasins et anticipait désormais au moins 125 fermetures nettes sur l’exercice 2026.
PRESSION SUR DEMNA Kering a nommé l'an dernier Luca de Meo pour restructurer le groupe. Après une hausse initiale à l'annonce de son arrivée, le titre Kering a perdu de son élan. L'action affiche un recul d'environ 8% sur un an, dans un contexte de repli plus général du secteur du luxe.
Luca de Meo vise à doubler la marge opérationnelle de Kering d'ici à la fin de la décennie, à partir d'un niveau de 11,1% en 2025, grâce à des réductions de coûts, à de nouvelles fermetures de magasins et à une rationalisation de la chaîne d'approvisionnement.
Des analystes estiment toutefois que ces seules mesures d'efficacité ne suffiront pas à relancer des marques qui ont perdu de leur attrait.
Le directeur artistique de Saint Laurent, [USN:L8N45V0BG TEXT:"Anthony Vaccarello"], et [USN:FWN4611AW TEXT:"Sean McGirr"], d'Alexander McQueen, ont tous deux quitté leurs fonctions ce mois-ci.
Les médias spécialisés spéculent également sur l'avenir de Pierpaolo Piccioli, directeur artistique de Balenciaga.
Ces changements devraient accentuer encore la pression sur Demna, qui s'apprête à boucler sa première année complète à la tête de Gucci, qu'il a cherché à relancer en misant sur une esthétique audacieuse et sensuelle rappelant les succès de la marque sous Tom Ford.
Demna a également adopté une approche inhabituelle en matière de production, en délocalisant en Chine la fabrication de ses premiers modèles de baskets.

Oct 22 : AI safety evaluators METR and Redwood Research found several new vulnerabilities in OpenAI's internal system, including an exploit agents could have used to keep hundreds of their actions from being monitored, in a pilot review earlier this year.
The exercise, conducted from July 21 to August 11, gave outside researchers "a deep level of access" to OpenAI's internal infrastructure for so-called embedded evaluations, the safety nonprofits said on Thursday.
METR and Redwood said they each sent one researcher, tested an arrangement giving access to OpenAI's internal code, documentation and some technical staff. Both were accompanied on site and used OpenAI-issued devices that "never left the premises".
OpenAI told the safety organizations it has since patched all vulnerabilities affecting its production safeguards, although METR and Redwood said they had not verified the fixes.

AI labs, experts and the Trump administration have touted independent evaluation by outside reviewers as a way to safely advance the technology without slowing its development.
However, AI companies are worried that evaluator staff working inside the companies' walls could take proprietary information to rivals, Reuters reported earlier this month.
While OpenAI received a full 61-page internal report, METR and Redwood said they agreed to publish only a broad summary publicly, and gave OpenAI the right to redact sensitive information.
Unlike in some previous evaluations, they could not independently disclose those redactions, but said they expected greater transparency in future evaluations.
The researchers also identified a potential way for OpenAI's Codex agents to bypass security restrictions and act with their users' full permissions.
The evaluators assessed the monitoring system as it existed on and before July 21, and noted that OpenAI was expanding the system during the exercise.
OpenAI said the "findings helped strengthen safeguards as we expanded the system and will help shape future research collaborations with METR and other third-party evaluators."

items.title: Ahead of the US midterms, Gen Z investors are making portfolio changes
items.author: Hani Richter
items.creator: Hani Richter
items.summary: Brandon Gaw is monitoring the news to adjust investments that he thinks could be hit hard by pre-election volatility ahead of the US midterms.
items.body:
Brandon Gaw, an Oregon-based engineering student and investor. Courtesy Brandon Gaw/Handout via REUTERS Brandon Gaw, an Oregon-based engineering student and investor, isn't just watching the news to stay in the know. He's also monitoring it to adjust investments that he thinks could be hit hard by pre-election volatility ahead of the US midterms .
“When others are fearful, that's the best time to invest,” he says.
One issue the 22-year-old is watching closely is the prospect of tighter restrictions involving Chinese-made memory chips entering the US market, as well as increased competition. Against this backdrop, Gaw says he is holding more cash and selling shares in smaller and newer companies that are more dependent on investors' excitement about AI, which he believes could be especially vulnerable to election uncertainty. Every few weeks, Gaw trades stocks worth $5,000 to $10,000. “In my opinion, those are going to get hit the most,” he says.
Brandon Gaw, an Oregon-based engineering student and investor. Courtesy Brandon Gaw/Handout via REUTERS Gaw accepts he’s taking more risk because of his age compared to an investor who may need their money sooner for retirement or a house. But he’s also investing in more established companies, including Microsoft, Google, Nvidia and Apple. “If anything, I added a few more positions in those companies,” he says. “I don't think they're going to run out of business anytime soon.”
For now, Gaw’s portfolio is fairly spread out: crypto, gold and silver collectively account for about 5% to 10%; ETFs make up around 30%; and individual stocks account for 60%. He has not made changes to his retirement investments. Taking a long-term view, Gaw says a market dip does not matter much to him if the S&P 500 falls. “I think these pullbacks are pretty good buying opportunities,” he says.
THE WIDER TREND
Nearly three-quarters of Gen Z investors have changed their retirement savings or portfolios in anticipation of the midterm election outcomes, compared to just 17% of Baby Boomers, according to a recent Nationwide Retirement Institute survey of over 2,000 US investors.
Tyler McConville, a Wisconsin-based certified financial planner and private wealth advisor at Capital Group, says “The challenge is determining which information actually matters to a long-term financial plan.”
While it is important to pay attention to elections and policy changes, markets have historically been influenced more by economic fundamentals and specific policy outcomes. “The biggest risk is when investors make long-term portfolio decisions based on short-term political concerns,” he says.
KEY TAKEAWAYS
Don’t make speculative trades. Use market-moving events as a reminder to review your investments and to consider how elections could affect certain sectors.
Keep diversification in mind. Gaw spreads his investments across individual stocks, ETFs, crypto and precious metals, while reducing his exposure to stocks that he considers volatile. A diversified portfolio can help limit reliance on any one investment or sector.
Focus on economic fundamentals. Rather than assuming one political party will be good or bad for stocks, consider factors such as inflation, interest rates, corporate earnings and specific policy changes when assessing your investments.
Have a money lesson or story to share? Tell us what worked for you — or what didn’t — by emailing hani.richter@tr.com .

items.title: Japan to arrange private investments worth $6.36 billion in Bangladesh, Nikkei reports
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Japan will agree to arrange 1 trillion yen ($6.36 billion) in private-sector investments in Bangladesh over the next five years, the Nikkei newspaper reported on Thursday.
items.body:
Japan will agree to arrange 1 trillion yen ($6.36 billion) in private-sector investments in Bangladesh over the next five years, the Nikkei newspaper reported on Thursday.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi will host her Bangladesh counterpart Tarique Rahman for a summit in Japan this month, and a joint statement will mention the arrangement, the report said.
The investments are expected to go into automobile and other manufacturing industries, as well as the construction of energy facilities, Nikkei reported.
It will also involve companies entering the Bangladesh Special Economic Zone being developed by parties including Japanese trading house Sumitomo Corp (8053.T) , the newspaper added.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
($1 = 157.1900 yen)

FAST

Oct 22 : Cable production capacity is emerging as a bottleneck for AI-driven data centre construction, Nexans' finance chief said, as demand rises faster than the industry's ability to expand manufacturing capacity.
Global cable capacity is tight and building a new cross-linked polyethylene (XLPE) cable production line, known in the industry as a CV line, takes around three years, limiting how quickly suppliers can respond to demand, Nexans CFO Vincent Piquet told Reuters.
"Things can't move quickly and the people building these data centres are in a great hurry," Piquet said.
Data centres require large amounts of low- and medium-voltage cable to connect power infrastructure, with larger facilities consuming proportionately more medium-voltage cable.

The strain on power infrastructure is already delaying some projects. In September, Oracle issued a force majeure notice to a Blue Owl unit developing a large data centre in New Mexico, citing potential difficulties securing sufficient power for the site.
Piquet said grid constraints, while slowing some projects, were also supporting demand for Nexans' products and allowing the company to be more selective when allocating capacity.
French distribution network operator Enedis has moved from annual procurement agreements to contracts lasting six or seven years in order to secure cable supply, he said.
While Europe generally faces fewer grid-connection challenges than the United States and benefits from stronger electricity networks in some northern countries, Piquet said lengthy regulatory processes were delaying certain projects.
He said he did not expect demand linked to artificial intelligence to slow, although Europe's data-centre expansion was likely to be less pronounced than in the United States because private investment capacity was smaller and public funding played a larger role.

items.title: South Africa’s Trade With China Surges After Beijing’s Zero-Tariff Deal
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: South Africa’s trade with China has increased since Beijing introduced a temporary zero-tariff scheme for qualifying South African exports in May, offering Pretoria an opportunity to expand sales to its largest trading partner as relations with the United States come under increasing strain. South African …
items.summary_source: The China-Global South Project source metadata
items.body:
South Africa’s trade with China has increased since Beijing introduced a temporary zero-tariff scheme for qualifying South African exports in May, offering Pretoria an opportunity to expand sales to its largest trading partner as relations with the United States come under increasing strain.

South African exports to China rose nearly 25% year over year between May and August, while imports from China increased 23% over the same period, Chinese Ambassador Wu Peng said at an event in Pretoria on Thursday.

South Africa has been seeking to rebalance its trade with China, which is its largest trading partner. In 2025, South Africa exported about 222 billion rand ($13.5 billion) worth of goods to China and imported nearly twice that amount, Trade Minister Parks Tau said.

South Africa’s exports to China include agricultural products, minerals and manufactured goods. The government is seeking to expand access for higher-value products as it looks to narrow the trade imbalance and diversify its export markets.

Wu said he had heard South Africa’s concerns about the imbalance in bilateral trade and expressed confidence that Chinese market access for South African products would expand.

“I am confident more and more South African high value-added products will enter the Chinese market in the future,” he said.

China’s zero-tariff preference scheme took effect on May 1, 2026, and is scheduled to run through April 30, 2028, pending a broader economic partnership arrangement between China and African countries. The temporary measure covers qualifying South African exports that meet applicable rules of origin and documentation requirements, while certain products are subject to tariff-rate quotas.

The arrangement provides South African exporters with an opportunity to compete in the Chinese market without paying customs duties on eligible goods. However, the increase in trade recorded since May does not establish how much of the growth resulted directly from the tariff changes.

For Pretoria, expanding exports to China is part of a broader effort to develop alternative markets as uncertainty over access to the U.S. market threatens an established source of export demand.

The United States has extended the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), which gives eligible sub-Saharan African countries duty-free access to the U.S. market for thousands of products, through 2028. South Africa, however, faces the risk of exclusion as President Donald Trump’s administration has criticized several of its domestic and foreign policies.

The Trump administration has accused the South African government of persecuting white people, an allegation Pretoria denies.

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said on October 19 that the country must prepare for the possibility of losing its AGOA benefits, as his government pursues alternative markets and holds discussions with U.S. counterparts.

Tau said he expected an announcement in early November on whether South Africa would be excluded from the program, but remained “cautiously optimistic.”

The uncertainty has added urgency to South Africa’s efforts to diversify its export destinations, including through stronger commercial ties with China. However, expanding trade with Beijing does not necessarily guarantee a reduction in the bilateral trade imbalance, particularly as imports from China are also rising.

South Africa’s ability to benefit from the Chinese scheme will depend partly on whether domestic producers can increase exports of qualifying goods and move into higher-value agricultural, industrial and processed products. The tariff preference removes customs duties on eligible exports but does not eliminate other market-access requirements.

The two countries’ trade figures point to expanding commercial ties, but the challenge for Pretoria will be to translate that growth into greater export earnings and a more balanced trading relationship.

With a decision on South Africa’s AGOA eligibility expected in early November, the country faces pressure to strengthen its position in China and other markets while seeking to preserve preferential access to the United States.

items.title: Anthropic IPO stands alone as AI market jitters sideline others
items.author: Echo Wang
items.creator: Echo Wang
items.summary: A once-robust fall calendar for technology IPOs is down to just Anthropic.
items.body:
A once-robust fall calendar for technology IPOs is down to just Anthropic.
The AI lab is pressing ahead to hold its initial public offering as planned in the middle of next month after making its prospectus public as early as late October, people familiar with the matter said, cautioning the plan and the dates are subject to change.
Anthropic's planned IPO will test whether its position at the center of the booming AI business, which some investors believe to deem worthy of a potential $1.5 trillion valuation, can overcome a market environment that might typically prompt bankers and deal lawyers to counsel delay. Anthropic is expected to begin marketing its shares to prospective investors during the week of November 9, one of the people said.
Other companies in the artificial intelligence infrastructure and data center sectors have delayed their listings, facing a rise in interest rates that has helped fuel a punishing selloff in shares and bonds of AI operators such as CoreWeave (CRWV.O) and broader questions about the sustainability of AI spending.
The contrast underscores Anthropic's appeal to investors even as concerns about competition from open-source models and AI safety weigh on the sector.
Many large investors remain bullish on Anthropic’s prospects despite the fall turbulence, viewing the firm as one of the few opportunities to gain exposure to a technology sector that long-term investors cannot afford to ignore. Other issuers are reluctant to compete with Anthropic for institutional investors' attention and capital, two of the people said.
Anthropic declined to comment.
VALUATIONS COMING UNDER PRESSURE The AI sector pullback follows a string of IPO delays and withdrawals since September, as market volatility and rising interest rates have made it harder for companies to secure attractive valuations.
Switch, a data center operator, and Nscale, an AI infrastructure provider, have pushed their IPO plans back to later this year, people familiar with the matter said, while stressing that plans remain fluid and subject to change. Nscale’s delay was partly driven by the need to address comments from SEC staff, one other person said. SoftBank-backed SB Energy has also postponed its listing, Reuters previously reported.
NScale declined to comment. Switch didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Blackstone-backed [USN:L6N45Z09R TEXT:"AirTrunk REIT"] and Nvidia (NVDA.O) -backed [USN:P8N42P0IJ TEXT:"Firmus"] have pulled or paused their offerings, Reuters has reported.
Oura's recent IPO has added to the caution among prospective issuers. The offering attracted little participation from long-only investors, a person familiar with the matter said, raising concerns about the depth of demand from institutional investors that typically provide a stable base of shareholders for newly listed companies.
SCRUTINY ON MULTIPLE FRONTS The retreat from AI infrastructure listings reflects growing scrutiny of the enormous capital required to build data centers and whether future demand will justify the investment.
Recent developments involving CoreWeave have added to concerns about a potential slowdown in AI spending, although some market participants do not expect such a downturn to materialize.
Nscale publicly filed its IPO registration statement in September, while Switch submitted its filing confidentially, Reuters reported previously. A confidential filing allows a company to work with regulators on its registration statement before disclosing financial and business details to the public. Companies typically publish the filing ahead of investor roadshows, when they begin marketing shares to prospective investors.

items.title: Will US Treasury scrap 20-year bond sales?
items.author: Jamie McGeever
items.creator: Jamie McGeever
items.summary: The US Treasury's auction of 20-year bonds on Wednesday won’t be the last, but this long-term debt instrument's days may be numbered.
items.body:
The US Treasury's auction of 20-year bonds on Wednesday won’t be the last, but this long-term debt instrument's days may be numbered.
Long-term borrowing costs are high. Yields on 10-year and 30-year Treasuries earlier this month rose to their highest levels since 2002, reaching 5.36% and 5.66%, respectively. The 5.469% that Treasury paid to borrow $13 billion on Wednesday was the highest yield at a 20-year auction since 1986. Discussion of whether the government should scrap this less liquid maturity altogether has intensified recently.
Meanwhile, US federal debt has crossed the $40 trillion threshold, while Washington's interest bill for fiscal 2026 hit a record $1.36 trillion, putting interest payments as a share of GDP at a historic high of 3.2%. These metrics are all rising.
When debt is above $40 trillion, a few basis points lower in borrowing costs can save billions. This points to an obvious strategy for lowering average government borrowing costs: lighten the load at the long end of the curve and borrow more at the front, where rates are lower.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent appears intent on doing just that. In August, Treasury announced it would at least double its $2 billion scheduled buybacks of longer-dated debt, referring to 10-year notes and 20- and 30-year bonds. It later increased that to $6 billion.
Treasury said this reflected its "desire to provide greater liquidity support" to certain parts of the curve. That may be true, but it also just happens to align with longer-term efforts to shorten Treasury’s maturity profile. Around 22% of US public debt is currently in T-bills, which mature in one year or less, compared with around 15% five years ago.
This is far from a “risk-free” strategy. By increasing the share of short-term debt, the government gives up the security of longer-term financing, meaning it must refinance more often. This "rollover risk" exposes the government to bouts of market shocks or volatility.
But Bessent has few options.
DEAR PRUDENCE A sudden burst of deficit-reduction fervor could sweep across Washington, leading to huge spending cuts or large tax hikes. But that's unlikely.
The US budget deficit hit $2 trillion in fiscal 2026, more than 6% of GDP, and there is little appetite in the White House to tackle it. President Donald Trump recently pledged to mail $5,000 checks to every adult in the country if his Republican Party wins both houses of Congress in the midterm elections on November 3, a splurge that would cost over $1.1 trillion, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget.
Absent serious belt-tightening, Treasury has to consider other measures to help lower long-term borrowing costs.
One could be reducing sales of the 20-year bond or getting rid of it entirely. The 20-year is one of the least liquid parts of the yield curve, with a limited supply of natural buyers. That means the government often has to offer a slightly more attractive yield.
Markets will find out more in the first week of November when Treasury unveils its quarterly refunding plans.
What can we expect?
Normally, very little. In the words of the Treasury itself, the debt auction process, calendar and issuance amounts should be “regular and predictable” to ensure smooth functioning of the world's largest and most important market. But these are not normal times.
The Treasury’s $6 billion accelerated buyback plan proved to be a bit of a flop, as the government failed to purchase the full amount in the first two rounds of buybacks in September. More importantly, long-dated yields rose as much as 50 basis points following the buyback announcement.
Citi's US rates strategists expect 20-year and 30-year auction sizes to be reduced by $3 billion, with the gap filled by additional bill issuance. Treasury may also opt for more flexibility by keeping auction sizes unchanged but signaling that future adjustments are in play.
Alternatively, Treasury may decide to retain the status quo. Analysts at JPMorgan reckon the scale of borrowing required in the coming years is so huge that it would "not be prudent" to discontinue a "critical" source of funding from an instrument that raises $168 billion a year. What's more, yields might be high, but they're not disconnected from current economic fundamentals, they argue.
Given that the midterm elections are also in the first week of November, Treasury’s quarterly refunding plan may not be absolutely top of mind for investors. But that might be a mistake, as subtle changes in the government’s funding strategy could have big implications down the line.
(The opinions expressed here are those of the author, a columnist for Reuters)

items.title: Ebola patient in Nigeria believed to have contracted disease in Uganda, Switzerland says
items.author: The Straits Times
items.summary: DAKAR, Oct 22 - The Ebola patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, is believed to have contracted the disease while travelling in Uganda, a Swiss government statement to Reuters said on Thursday.
items.body:
Ebola patient in Nigeria believed to have contracted disease in Uganda, Switzerland says
Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

Published   Oct 22, 2026, 08:41 PM

Updated   Oct 23, 2026, 03:01 AM

Set as preferred source

Listen

DAKAR, Oct 22 - The Ebola patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, is believed to have contracted the disease while travelling in Uganda, a Swiss government statement to Reuters said on Thursday.
Nigeria reported the case, its first Ebola case in more than a decade, on Tuesday, becoming the fourth African country and the most populous yet to be affected by an outbreak that was announced in Democratic Republic of Congo in mid-May and has since become the fastest-spreading on record.
Ugandan authorities have said the woman who fell ill in Nigeria had travelled to eastern Congo before transiting through Uganda. But the World Health Organization and Africa's top health agency said on Thursday they had not received confirmed information that the woman had travelled to Congo.

The woman "has been in a private clinic in Abuja for around a week with symptoms. She is believed to have contracted the virus whilst travelling to Uganda around two weeks ago," said an emailed statement from the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs.
"Her husband is in isolation; he has not shown any symptoms. He was travelling with his wife when she is believed to have contracted Ebola."
Uganda reported 20 cases in May and June, mostly imported from Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country Ebola-free in August.

Ugandan government spokesperson Alan Kasujja told Reuters late on Thursday that Uganda had no Ebola cases.
"That's a fact. If we did, as has happened before, we'd be the first to say," he said.
Asked whether the Ugandan government had proof that the woman had travelled to Congo, Kasujja said, "Like what? A passport stamp? Without infringing on the patient’s rights?"

AFRICA CDC, WHO SAY NO INFORMATION THAT PATIENT WENT TO CONGO
Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention official Wessam Mankoula said on Thursday that Nigeria and Uganda were sharing information to establish the patient's movements and possible source of exposure.
"So far, there is no validated information (that) this case traveled to DRC (Democratic Republic of Congo)," Mankoula told an online press conference.
The WHO said information it had received about the case did not include travel outside Uganda.
"The facts which we have received is that the patient returned to Abuja on October 3, being away from September 16 in Uganda," WHO representative to Nigeria Pavel Ursu told the press conference.
Ursu said the focus in Nigeria was now on containing the viral infection and that the patient remained hospitalised, with her biochemical markers improving.
Jean Kaseya, Africa CDC director, told Reuters on Wednesday that the patient had been on a two-week holiday in Uganda.
Patrick Otim, a WHO emergency response manager, said on Thursday the source of her infection was still unknown as health authorities were working to piece together her travel history.
One issue under investigation is which health facilities the woman visited in Abuja after the onset of her symptoms and before her hospitalisation 48 hours later, Otim said.
KENYA TRACES ALL CONTACTS OF FIRST CASE
Separately, a senior Kenyan health official said authorities there had now traced all 135 contacts of the country's first Ebola case, which was confirmed on October 6 and after which a further eight cases have been reported.
"We have been able to account for them 100%," health ministry director-general Patrick Amoth said. He said the last contact to be traced was a Ugandan citizen who had arrived in Kenya in early October on the same flight as the index patient but exited by road via the Namanga border post with Tanzania, which meant it took more time to find him.
Africa CDC is investigating whether the Kenyan case may have come into contact with the patient being treated in Nigeria, as both travelled from Uganda's Entebbe airport on the same day, Mankoula said. Transmission between the two was one of the possible scenarios being examined, he said.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people, whether living or dead. The disease can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding.
The rare Ebola species behind the current outbreak kills about half of those infected and has no approved treatment or vaccine.
So far the outbreak is confirmed to have killed about 4,700 people across the four African countries that have reported cases, according to the Africa CDC. REUTERS
